# National Geographic Society Headquarters

The National Geographic Society Headquarters is a historic complex occupying a full city block in downtown Washington, D.C., serving as the central hub for one of the world's most prominent non-profit organizations dedicated to exploration, science, and education , . Officially located at 1145 17th Street NW, the campus is affectionately known as the "Home of the Explorer" and represents a physical manifestation of the society's mission to inspire global stewardship and foster an "Explorer Mindset" , . The headquarters is not a single structure but a multi-building campus that has evolved over more than a century, reflecting the growth of the organization itself from an academic club to a global institution. This evolution is most clearly visible in its architecture, which spans several distinct styles, from Italian Renaissance Revival to modernist New Formalism . The campus has been officially recognized for its cultural significance, having been listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 5, 2023 . For decades, it has functioned as both a private operational base for the society's staff and a public-facing destination, housing the National Geographic Museum, which offers free admission to changing and permanent exhibitions , . In recent years, the headquarters has entered a new phase of development with a monumental $250 million transformation project scheduled for completion in mid-2026 , . This expansion, known as 'Base Camp' or the 'Museum of Exploration', aims to create a unified, immersive experience that quadruples the society's public space and integrates the entire historic campus into a cohesive visitor destination , . The project incorporates state-of-the-art digital fabrication technologies, ambitious sustainability goals targeting LEED Platinum certification, and a comprehensive suite of inclusive design features, positioning the campus as a model for modern cultural institutions , .

## Foundational Campus and Architectural Heritage

The physical home of the National Geographic Society began its life not as a grand headquarters, but as a modest hall constructed to house the burgeoning activities of a scholarly society founded in the nation's capital. The story of the current headquarters campus begins in 1888, when the National Geographic Society was established in Washington, D.C., by a charter group of 33 men, including explorers, scientists, and educators , , . Its first president, Gardiner Greene Hubbard, a lawyer and philanthropist, was elected to lead the organization with the specific goal of promoting geographical knowledge to a wider audience , . Initially, the society operated from rented offices, but it quickly outgrew these temporary quarters . The cornerstone for its permanent home, named Hubbard Memorial Hall in honor of its first president, was laid in early 1902, with the five-month-old great-grandson of President Hubbard participating in the ceremony . Construction continued through 1903, and the main building, completed in 1904, became the foundational element of the society's physical presence in the city , . This initial structure, designed by the firm Hornblower & Marshall, established the campus's architectural character and set the stage for future expansions . The building was constructed in the Italian Renaissance style, featuring buff brick, limestone detailing, and a distinctive red terracotta hipped roof . Inside, it housed murals painted by the renowned illustrator N.C. Wyeth between 1926 and 1927, adding a layer of artistic prestige to the functional space . This original building served as the home base for explorers who returned from their expeditions to share their findings and stories, cementing its role as the "Home of the Explorer" from its inception , .

As the National Geographic Society grew, its administrative needs expanded beyond the capacity of Hubbard Hall. The next major phase of construction involved the creation of the Administration Building, a structure that would come to define the southern edge of the campus and reflect the organization's increasing stature. Designed by architect Arthur B. Heaton, this building was constructed in two distinct stages . The northern wing was completed in 1912–1913, followed by the south wing and the connecting central pavilion in 1931–1932 , . Built in the Neoclassical style, the Administration Building presented a stately and authoritative facade to the city, clad in buff brick and punctuated by imposing Ionic columns . Its marble lobby featured an elegant embossed brass world globe and a star motif, symbols of the society's global mission . This addition transformed the campus from a singular hall into a connected complex, providing essential office space and creating a more formal institutional presence. The combination of the earlier Italian Renaissance-style Hubbard Hall and the later Neoclassical Administration Building created a rich architectural dialogue that reflected the society's deep roots and its growing influence in the fields of geography and exploration. Together, these two buildings formed the core of the campus until the mid-20th century, contributing to the Sixteenth Street Historic District, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978 . Their collective listing on the NRHP in 2023 underscores their enduring historical and architectural value .

The architectural narrative of the headquarters campus was dramatically altered in the mid-20th century with the arrival of a modernist masterpiece. The Edward Durell Stone-designed building, completed in 1964, represented a bold departure from the traditional styles of its predecessors and symbolized the society's dynamic expansion during the presidency of Melville Bell Grosvenor (1957–1967) , . Stone, a leading proponent of New Formalism, created a ten-story white marble-clad reinforced concrete structure that reoriented the campus's primary orientation to 17th Street . His design skillfully adapted classical architectural forms—specifically the column's base-shaft-capital—to a modern skyscraper, resulting in a building that was simultaneously classic and contemporary . The structure featured vertical marble piers, bronze-framed windows, and black granite spandrels, all contributing to a sense of refined elegance and structural clarity . This building, documented in architectural archives and photographed during its construction in 1963, was a significant project in Stone's portfolio, alongside corporate commissions for giants like General Motors and Standard Oil , . It stands as a prime example of the shift toward an elegant, classically influenced modernism that characterized American architecture in the mid-20th century . The addition of this modernist tower completed the four-building complex that defined the headquarters for much of the latter half of the 20th century, creating a diverse architectural tapestry that told the story of the society's journey from a small club to a global powerhouse. The final pre-expansion building was added in 1984, further modernizing the campus and preparing it for another era of change , . The entire complex, comprising these four distinct buildings, collectively received its own listing on the National Register of Historic Places in 2023, formally recognizing its unique contribution to American architectural history .

This carefully curated collection of buildings tells a story of growth, adaptation, and architectural evolution. From the intimate, scholarly feel of Hubbard Hall to the grand authority of the Administration Building and the sleek modernity of the Stone Building, each structure contributes to the campus's identity. The designation of the entire complex as a historic place validates its role not just as an organizational headquarters, but as a significant piece of American architectural heritage .

## Mid-Century Expansion and Modernization

The mid-20th century marked a period of profound transformation for the National Geographic Society, a change vividly mirrored in the architectural expansion of its Washington, D.C. headquarters. The most significant development of this era was the construction of the Edward Durell Stone-designed building, a project that fundamentally reshaped the campus and its public profile . As the society's international reach and financial resources grew under the leadership of President Melville Bell Grosvenor, the need for more expansive and modern office space became critical . Stone’s design, completed in 1964, responded directly to this need while also aligning with the broader architectural currents of the time , . The building, a ten-story tower of white marble, stood in stark contrast to the older, more traditional styles of Hubbard Hall and the Administration Building . It embodied the principles of New Formalism, a movement championed by Stone that sought to reconcile classical architectural language with modern materials and technology , . By translating the proportions and rhythms of a classical column into the vertical bays of a skyscraper, Stone created a structure that felt both timeless and forward-looking . This new building not only provided much-needed space but also served as a powerful symbol of the society's dynamism and its commitment to progress in the post-war world . The construction process itself was well-documented, with photographs capturing the building rising from the ground in 1963, highlighting its emergence as a new landmark on the cityscape . The dedication of this modernist icon in 1964 solidified the headquarters as a center for exploration and discovery in the contemporary era .

Following the completion of the Stone Building, the campus underwent another significant modification in the late 1970s. A fourth building, designed by the influential architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM), was added to the complex in 1984 , . This addition brought a new dimension to the campus, incorporating multifunctional spaces that enhanced both its internal operations and its relationship with the surrounding city. The SOM-designed building featured a 400-seat theater, a vital component for screening films and hosting lectures, and a publicly accessible outdoor plaza, creating a more welcoming and integrated environment . This plaza became a notable feature of the campus, distinguished by its thoughtful landscape design. In 1984, the society commissioned artist Elyn Zimmerman to create a sculptural installation for the space, resulting in the work *Marabar* , . The installation consisted of a long, narrow reflecting pool set among five large South Dakota granite boulders, one of which was highly polished to act as a mirror, reflecting the others and the sky , . The name, drawn from E.M. Forster's novel *A Passage to India*, and the site-specific nature of the work made it a culturally significant piece . The plaza's design intentionally used natural elements like the granite boulders to appear older than the built environment, creating a contemplative and timeless atmosphere . This addition by SOM, along with the existing buildings, completed the headquarters campus as it existed for several decades, forming a cohesive yet diverse ensemble of architectural styles that reflected the society's long and varied history.

The campus also served as a crucible for technological innovation, a function deeply intertwined with the society's mission to document the world. Long before the modern expansion, the headquarters housed a photo engineering lab in its basement where custom imaging technology had been developed continuously since at least the early 1900s . This legacy of in-house technical expertise was famously demonstrated in 1960, when Jacques Cousteau presented groundbreaking underwater film footage at the headquarters . The presentation was made possible through a collaboration between Cousteau and Harold Edgerton, a professor at MIT who was funded by the National Geographic Society . Edgerton showcased specialized electronic flash lighting systems he had developed, which were attached to a sled and allowed for high-quality photography in the dark depths of the ocean . This event underscored the headquarters' role not just as an administrative center, but as a hub for pioneering research and the advancement of visual storytelling. The society's commitment to innovation extended to motion pictures, which it began producing in 1903 and 1908, archiving them at the headquarters even though the bulk of the collection is now stored off-site in Pennsylvania . This history of technical experimentation positioned the National Geographic brand as a leader in visual media, a reputation that continues to be cultivated within its modern exhibition spaces. The campus, therefore, was not merely a container for the organization's work but an active participant in its creative and scientific processes. The combination of architectural expansion, cultural landscaping, and technological advancement in the mid-to-late 20th century cemented the headquarters as a vital and evolving institution, perfectly poised for the next chapter of its history.

## The Contemporary Campus: Operations and Public Engagement

Today, the National Geographic Society Headquarters continues to serve as the nerve center for the organization, functioning as the official headquarters for its Education and Community Engagement division . This division is responsible for strategic planning, program management, and coordinating explorer-related activities across the greater Washington, D.C. area, encompassing the District of Columbia, Maryland, and Virginia . On-site staff play a crucial role in supporting the society's global mission, managing logistics for explorers traveling to field sites—including visa processing and per diem coordination—and overseeing accessibility initiatives to ensure the society's programs are inclusive . The campus provides the essential infrastructure for these operations, housing the offices and meeting spaces necessary for the society's approximately 1,200 employees, a number reported in the late 1990s . Beyond its administrative functions, the headquarters has long been a destination for those seeking to engage with the world's wonders. The National Geographic Museum, situated within the headquarters complex at 1145 17th Street NW, serves as the primary public-facing component of the campus , . Located on the first floor of the complex, the museum is open daily and offers free admission to its visitors, making the society's vast collections and compelling narratives widely accessible , . The museum presents a dynamic mix of changing exhibitions and permanent displays that reflect the society's core focus on global expeditions, scientific research, and adventure , . These exhibitions often feature iconic artifacts, such as Robert Peary’s camera from his North Pole expedition and pottery recovered by Jacques Cousteau from a shipwreck, providing tangible connections to historic moments of discovery , . The museum also showcases rotating exhibits on a wide range of topics, from the untold story of pirate ships to ancient Egyptian treasures, using immersive audiovisual elements and interactive learning stations to captivate audiences of all ages , .

The headquarters has also played a pivotal role as a pedagogical site, offering unique educational opportunities that extend beyond its museum walls. The campus has hosted events like the 2018 workshop for middle school students from MacFarland Middle School and School Without Walls at Francis Stevens . During this three-day event, students participated in screenings of Pulitzer Center-funded films published in National Geographic, engaged in facilitated film analysis with journalists, and worked on curriculum-aligned media literacy instruction . Such programs demonstrate the headquarters' function as a living classroom, where students can learn about underreported issues through the lens of documentary filmmaking and journalism . Furthermore, behind-the-scenes tours of the campus provide glimpses into areas not typically open to the public, such as the historic stage where explorers like Jacques Cousteau and Jane Goodall once presented their findings, and the National Geographic Museum's impressive collection of magazines spanning the society's entire publication history . The campus also supports ongoing conservation efforts, such as Joel Sartore's Photo Ark project, a multiyear initiative to photograph every species in captivity, which is hosted and promoted from the headquarters as part of its public engagement programming . Through these diverse functions, the headquarters operates as a hybrid space: a private operational base for the society's global endeavors and a vibrant public institution dedicated to education, inspiration, and community engagement. This dual role is central to its identity and ensures its continued relevance as a cultural landmark in Washington, D.C.

One of the most intriguing historical aspects of the headquarters is its connection to the Cold War era. In the 1960s, the complex contained a Cold War-era fallout shelter equipped with an integrated morgue . Unlike many of the more austere shelters found in the city, this facility was reportedly quite comfortable, featuring cots, showers, medical supplies, and even toothpaste, earning it the informal description of a "five-star fallout shelter" in a 1982 news feature . This detail highlights the headquarters' role as a secure and self-sufficient institution, prepared for a range of potential emergencies. The campus has also served as a literal home for some of the society's most intrepid explorers. Hiram Bingham, the discoverer of Machu Picchu, and J. Michael Fay, a noted conservationist, were both known to have slept overnight in the Society's buildings while in Washington on assignment during the 2000s . This tradition of accommodating explorers underscores the headquarters' status as a true home base—a sanctuary and launching point for those pushing the boundaries of human knowledge and endurance. The campus has also been a venue for public events and celebrations, such as the "Grosvenor Council Curated Tour" offered to select members, confirming that the building remains open for in-person visits by a limited, invited audience as of 2024–2025 . This blend of security, hospitality, and public service reflects the multifaceted nature of the headquarters as an institution that must balance the demands of secrecy and safety with its mission of openness and global outreach.

The campus has also demonstrated a long-standing commitment to environmental responsibility. In 2004, the headquarters building became one of the first in the region to receive a "Green" certification from Global Green USA, acknowledging its adherence to high standards of environmental sustainability , . This early recognition signaled a forward-thinking approach to building management that has only intensified with the upcoming 'Base Camp' transformation. The new museum project explicitly targets LEED Platinum certification, the highest level of achievement in green building . This commitment is not merely symbolic; it is embedded in the project's detailed design. Specific sustainable strategies include the installation of solar panels that are expected to supply 25% of the campus's electric power, the use of bird-safe glass to mitigate avian collisions, and the implementation of a gray water HVAC system for energy efficiency , , . The project also includes a 45,000-gallon underground cistern for rainwater harvesting, which will be used for irrigation and other non-potable purposes . One particularly innovative choice involves the use of normal-weight concrete with standard cementitious fireproofing instead of carbon-intensive lightweight concrete, a decision that is projected to reduce emissions by 20% . These measures, combined with the repurposing of salvaged wood from trees killed by invasive beetles and the use of hot-dip galvanized steel for its durability, illustrate a holistic approach to sustainability that aligns the physical campus with the National Geographic brand's core values of science and conservation , . This integration of green building practices makes the headquarters a living testament to the organization's mission, transforming it from a static monument into a dynamic, environmentally conscious institution.

## The Base Camp Transformation and Future Vision

The National Geographic Society Headquarters is currently undergoing its most significant transformation in over a century, a $250 million project announced in late 2022 that will reshape the campus into a unified public destination , . This undertaking, referred to internally as "Base Camp," is described as the largest expansion in the society's 136-year history , . Scheduled for completion in mid-2026, the project will more than quadruple the society's downtown footprint, expanding its publicly accessible space from the existing museum to over 100,000 square feet , , . The transformation is led by architects Hickok Cole, Inc., known for designing the International Spy Museum, and involves the renovation and physical connection of all four original historic buildings, including Hubbard Hall, the Administration Building, and the M Street structures , , . The centerpiece of the project is a new 15,000-square-foot glass-facade pavilion, which will serve as the main entrance and event space and feature a rooftop terrace . This pavilion will anchor a new pedestrian plaza, reimagining the campus's streetscape and creating a cohesive gateway for visitors arriving from M Street . The project's vision is to create an immersive "explorer experience" that guides visitors from the bustling city into a world of discovery. The iconic yellow border of the National Geographic magazine, a familiar sight to millions, will be reinterpreted as an intentional architectural feature at the pavilion's entrance, signaling the start of the immersive journey , . The overall design draws inspiration from nature and employs cutting-edge digital fabrication technologies, robotics-assisted scanning, and BIM Level 400 modeling to achieve its ambitious goals , .

The new Museum of Exploration will feature a suite of state-of-the-art facilities designed to showcase the society's content in innovative ways. A key highlight will be a renovated 400-seat theater, equipped with cutting-edge storytelling tools for film screenings, lectures, and live programming , . The interior will host a variety of immersive and interactive exhibits. Among the most anticipated is the inaugural exhibition, "Photo Ark: Animals of Earth," created by photographer Joel Sartore, which will use large-scale wildlife projections, touch-responsive stations, and atmospheric audio cues to highlight the urgency of biodiversity loss . Another major exhibit will be the Rolex Explorers Landing, which will showcase historic expedition equipment and artifacts from the society's vast archives . The museum will also include a dedicated education center with "the learning launchpad" for students and school groups, a restaurant, a retail store, and a new café , , . Perhaps one of the most technologically advanced features will be the nighttime courtyard experience. This outdoor space will transform after dark into an immersive canvas for projection mapping, interactive media, and audioscapes, telling stories of exploration and discovery through light and sound , . This nightly show, beginning with an ocean-themed experience, promises to make the campus a vibrant cultural destination long after the indoor museum has closed . The project also includes a new store, a renovated theater, video wall, and expanded public archives, all designed to deepen the visitor's engagement with the National Geographic brand .

A core pillar of the Base Camp transformation is a profound commitment to inclusivity and accessibility, reflecting a modern sensibility in cultural institution design. The new museum will be equipped with a comprehensive suite of features intended to ensure the experience is welcoming and usable for people of all abilities and backgrounds. These include Braille instructional text throughout the exhibits, tactile and sensory maps for visually impaired visitors, and ASL interpretations of media content , , . Recognizing the diverse needs of visitors, the design incorporates all-gender restrooms, wellness rooms for nursing parents or individuals needing low-sensory time, and refrigerators for guest medication storage , , . To cater to a bilingual audience, the museum's content will be presented in both English and Spanish, and intuitive app support will provide visual descriptions for guests , . This deliberate focus on inclusivity is not an afterthought but a foundational design principle, aimed at fostering the "Explorer Mindset" universally and ensuring that exploration is perceived as a possibility for everyone . The project's planners emphasize that these features are integral to the museum's mission to cultivate curiosity and global understanding, positioning the National Geographic Society as a leader in progressive and equitable museum practices .

The tension between institutional development and the preservation of cultural heritage came to a head during the planning phase of the Base Camp project, particularly concerning the sculpture *Marabar*. When renderings for the new plaza were released in July 2024, the sculpture was conspicuously absent, prompting immediate concern from preservation advocates . The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) designated *Marabar* as a "Landslide" site, indicating it was at imminent risk of demolition, and initiated a formal review process with the District of Columbia’s Department of Consumer and Regulatory Affairs . The controversy escalated when the D.C. Historic Preservation Review Board rescinded its August 2024 approval for the plaza renovation, citing the artwork's cultural and landscape-architectural significance and urging the society to find a way to retain it on-site or justify why it could not be . This public pressure campaign, supported by figures like Whitney Museum Director Adam Weinberg, highlighted the deep value placed on the site-specific artwork . After years of advocacy and negotiation, the National Geographic Society reached a resolution. The society agreed to fund and execute the relocation of the massive sculpture under the direction of artist Elyn Zimmerman . The work, which weighs over one million pounds and is composed of five granite boulders arranged around a reflecting pool, was successfully moved in 2023 , . The reconfigured installation was reopened at American University on April 4, 2023, renamed *Sudama* , . While the resolution preserved the artwork, it underscored the complex negotiations required when a major institution undertakes a transformative project on a site rich with cultural layers. The episode serves as a case study in how public advocacy can influence the decisions of powerful organizations and highlights the delicate balance between progress and preservation.

## Architectural and Cultural Legacy

The National Geographic Society Headquarters campus stands as a remarkable archive of American architectural history, a testament to the society's evolution over more than a century. Its architectural diversity is not accidental but rather a direct reflection of the different eras in which it was built, each building embodying the prevailing aesthetic and technological trends of its time. The oldest components, Hubbard Hall (1904) and the Administration Building (1912–1932), represent the turn-of-the-century confidence of the Gilded Age and the early 20th century. Designed by Hornblower & Marshall and Arthur B. Heaton respectively, these structures draw upon classical European traditions—the Italian Renaissance Revival and Neoclassicism—to convey stability, authority, and scholarly gravitas . Their use of traditional materials like buff brick, limestone, and marble speaks to a desire for permanence and respectability, fitting for a young organization aiming to establish itself as a serious authority on geography . The subsequent addition of the Edward Durell Stone-designed building in 1964 marked a decisive break with the past, embracing the modernist ethos of the mid-20th century , . Stone’s New Formalism, evident in the white marble-clad tower, fused classical proportion with a clean, minimalist aesthetic, creating a building that was both rooted in history and pointed firmly towards the future . This structure, alongside the later 1984 addition by SOM, completed a campus that encapsulates the architectural arc from traditionalism to modernism, making it a valuable and coherent example of American architectural development , .

The campus's cultural legacy extends far beyond its architectural significance. It has been the physical heart of the National Geographic Society since its founding in 1888, a continuous presence in Washington, D.C.'s intellectual and cultural life , . For over a century, it has served as the "Home of the Explorer," a place where adventurers returned from the far corners of the globe to share their discoveries , . This tradition of storytelling has been central to the society's mission, and the headquarters has been the primary venue for these presentations, from Jacques Cousteau's underwater films to Jane Goodall's research on chimpanzees , . The campus has thus become a repository of human achievement, a space where the dramatic narratives of exploration have been translated into the stunning visuals and compelling articles that have defined the National Geographic brand for generations. The society's first magazine issue, printed in September 1888, was presented at meetings held at the Cosmos Club in Washington, D.C., establishing the city as the birthplace of its publishing enterprise . The headquarters has been the operational center for this enterprise ever since, housing the editorial teams, photographers, and scientists who have produced its iconic content , . This deep-rooted history makes the campus a living museum of the society's own story, preserving not just its artifacts but its very spirit of inquiry and wonder.

The campus has also been a site of important cultural and artistic interventions. The most prominent example is the relocation of Elyn Zimmerman's sculpture *Marabar* in 2023 . The controversy surrounding the planned removal of the 1984 installation and its subsequent successful relocation demonstrates the campus's role as a contested and evolving cultural landscape , . The preservation campaign led by TCLF and the intervention by the D.C. Historic Preservation Review Board elevated the conversation from a simple matter of campus redesign to a broader discussion about the value of public art and the responsibilities of cultural institutions , . The resolution, which resulted in the sculpture being given a new home at American University under the name *Sudama*, represents a significant moment in the history of both the sculpture and the headquarters . It illustrates the complex interplay between institutional ambition, public advocacy, and the enduring power of art to shape our perception of a place. While the sculpture no longer resides on the National Geographic campus, its story is now an integral part of the campus's cultural narrative, a reminder that even the most carefully planned transformations can be shaped by unexpected forces and that the preservation of cultural memory is an ongoing process. The campus, therefore, is not a static monument but a dynamic entity continually negotiating its past, present, and future.

To conclude, the National Geographic Society Headquarters is far more than a collection of buildings; it is a physical embodiment of the organization's identity. It is a historic complex that has grown alongside the society, its architecture telling the story of its expansion from a small scholarly club to a global institution. It is a functional hub, providing the operational backbone for one of the world's most respected non-profits. And it is a cherished public destination, inspiring generations of visitors through its museum, its exhibitions, and its commitment to storytelling. The forthcoming 'Base Camp' transformation will usher in a new chapter, integrating the campus into a seamless, immersive experience designed to foster a universal "Explorer Mindset." This expansion, guided by principles of sustainability, inclusivity, and cutting-edge technology, will build upon the rich architectural and cultural legacy of the site. The campus, with its diverse buildings, its storied history, and its future-oriented vision, remains a vital and evolving landmark, continuing its long tradition of exploring and communicating the world to all who visit.

## Historical Context and Organizational Evolution

The story of the National Geographic Society Headquarters is inextricably linked to the history of the organization itself. The society was founded on January 13, 1888, in Washington, D.C., by a charter group of 33 men, including prominent figures like Alexander Graham Bell and John Wesley Powell , . Incorporated on January 27, 1888, with the stated purpose of "the increase and diffusion of geographical knowledge," the society began its existence as a small academic club dedicated to the exchange of ideas among geographers, explorers, teachers, and cartographers , . The first president, Gardiner Greene Hubbard, was chosen precisely because he was not a scientist or geographer but a lawyer and philanthropist, a figure whose public-facing skills would help the society reach a broader audience . The society's first publications were academic articles originally presented at its meetings, held at venues like Columbia University and the Cosmos Club in Washington, D.C., before the society established its own permanent home . The first issue of *National Geographic Magazine* appeared eight months after the society's founding, in September 1888, printed in New Haven, Connecticut, and lacking the iconic yellow border that would become its trademark . This early history establishes Washington, D.C., as the undeniable cradle of the National Geographic brand, a fact that would eventually inform its choice of location for its headquarters.

Before settling into its definitive campus, the society occupied several locations as it grew. It operated from rented offices in the nation's capital before moving to its first permanent home at the corner of M Street and Sixteenth Street in 1903 , . This move to Hubbard Memorial Hall marked a significant milestone, providing a stable and dignified base for its expanding operations . An earlier functional headquarters was also located in Gaithersburg, Maryland, which served the society before its consolidation in Washington, D.C. . This building in Gaithersburg is noted to have been vacated prior to the consolidation, and it is now occupied by Montgomery County's Public Safety headquarters . The society's presence in Washington, D.C., has been unbroken since 1903, making the current headquarters campus a culmination of its long-term commitment to the nation's capital as a center for geographical inquiry and public education. The founding date of 1888 and the continuous operation from that city provide the chronological foundation for all subsequent developments at the headquarters, from the construction of Hubbard Hall in 1904 to the modernization projects of the 21st century , . The organization's annual sales were reported as $500 million in 1998, and it employed approximately 1,200 people in the late 1990s, underscoring its substantial growth and scale .

The evolution of the headquarters campus mirrors the evolution of the society's mission and methods. In its early decades, the headquarters was primarily an administrative and intellectual center. However, from its inception, it was also a hub for innovation in visual media. The society produced its first motion pictures in 1903 and 1908, creating silent, hand-cranked films to visually augment lectures . The first television documentary aired in 1963, narrated by Orson Welles . This commitment to visual storytelling was bolstered by the in-house photo engineering lab, which developed custom imaging technology since the early 1900s . This technical prowess was instrumental in enabling explorers to capture the world in new and compelling ways, from Harold Edgerton's underwater flashes for Jacques Cousteau to the high-resolution photography featured in the magazine today . The headquarters has thus always been a nexus of exploration, science, and technology, a place where scientific discovery meets creative expression. The physical campus, with its theaters, labs, and exhibition spaces, has provided the essential infrastructure for this interdisciplinary work.

In conclusion, the National Geographic Society Headquarters is a palimpsest, a layered record of the organization's remarkable journey. Each building and each renovation adds a new chapter to its story, documenting the society's transition from a niche scholarly society into a globally recognized institution dedicated to exploration and conservation. Its location in Washington, D.C., has been a constant, anchoring it to the seat of government and culture in the United States. The campus has witnessed the birth of the National Geographic Magazine, the rise of visual storytelling, the expansion of scientific research, and the deepening commitment to environmental sustainability and public education. The ongoing transformation into the Museum of Exploration is not a departure from this legacy but a continuation of it, representing the next step in the society's mission to inspire the explorer in all of us. The current headquarters campus is a culmination of its long-term commitment to the nation's capital as a center for geographical inquiry and public education.
The founding date of 1888 and the continuous operation from that city provide the chronological foundation for all subsequent developments at the headquarters.
The developments at the headquarters range from the construction of Hubbard Hall in 1904 to the modernization projects of the 21st century.
The organization's annual sales were reported as $500 million in 1998.
The National Geographic Society employed approximately 1,200 people in the late 1990s.
In its early decades, the headquarters was primarily an administrative and intellectual center.
From its inception, the headquarters was also a hub for innovation in visual media.
The society produced its first motion pictures in 1903 and 1908, creating silent, hand-cranked films to visually augment lectures.
The first television documentary aired in 1963, narrated by Orson Welles.
This commitment to visual storytelling was bolstered by the in-house photo engineering lab, which developed custom imaging technology since the early 1900s.
This technical prowess was instrumental in enabling explorers to capture the world in new and compelling ways.
The technical prowess enabled high-resolution photography featured in the magazine today.
The headquarters has always been a nexus of exploration, science, and technology.
The headquarters is a place where scientific discovery meets creative expression.
The physical campus, with its theaters, labs, and exhibition spaces, has provided the essential infrastructure for this interdisciplinary work.

![Image 1](https://images.nationalgeographic.org/dtpgi0zck/image/upload/t_news_ui_scale_by_height494/Courtyard_Daytime_1?_a=DAJHqpE+ZAA0)

Visualizations by REDVERTEX, based on designs by Hickok Cole, Inc.

**WASHINGTON, D.C., October 21, 2024** – Today, the National Geographic Society announced the launch of the National Geographic Museum of Exploration, a sustainably-built, must-visit experience as part of its reimagined campus in the heart of Washington, D.C. Scheduled to open in mid-2026, the public attraction, fueled by cutting-edge technologies, will feature one-of-a-kind National Geographic curated exhibitions, immersive and educational experiences, a state-of-the-art theater, restaurant and retail store.

The Museum of Exploration will accelerate the Society’s mission to illuminate and protect the wonder of our world. As a global nonprofit organization, the new Museum of Exploration is a pivotal step forward in the Society’s goal to build on its legacy of convening its global community of National Geographic Explorers — scientists, conservationists, storytellers and educators — who advance knowledge, inspire action and share their remarkable stories with the public.

Affectionately known as the “Home of the Explorer,” the Society’s historic headquarters occupies a city block in downtown Washington, D.C., and has evolved significantly over the past century. With support from JLL, HITT Contracting and Hickok Cole, the renovated public attraction will comprise over 100,000 square feet.

"The Museum of Exploration marks a historic chapter in the Society’s mission to advance exploration, science, education and storytelling, bringing these experiences to life in ways that spark curiosity, create lasting memories and invite everyone to embrace their inner Explorer,” said Jill Tiefenthaler, CEO of the National Geographic Society. “We’re excited to welcome visitors to experience our mission through immersive, unforgettable moments that deepen their connection to the wonder of our world.”

![Image 2](https://images.nationalgeographic.org/dtpgi0zck/image/upload/t_news_ui_scale_by_height494/Courtyard_Daytime_3?_a=DAJHqpE+ZAA0)

Visualizations by REDVERTEX, based on designs by Hickok Cole, Inc.

When visiting the Museum of Exploration, guests will enter through the 11-foot yellow border, discovering wonders of the world that the Society has illuminated for decades:

*   **Rolex Explorers Landing:** An exhibition dedicated to the innovative equipment and stories from awe-inspiring expeditions, featuring the work and artifacts of Explorers.
*   **Immersive Experience:** Visitors will have the chance to step into the role of an Explorer, immersing themselves in thrilling experiences and fieldwork in exciting and remote locations worldwide.
*   **State-of-the-Art Theater:** A 400-seat theater with innovations that will envelop visitors in stunning audiovisuals through National Geographic films and stories.
*   **Nighttime Courtyard Experience:** Washington, D.C.’s first spectacular outdoor nighttime experience that brings the wonder of our world to life through arresting visuals that National Geographic is known for, coupled with projection mapping, interactive media and audioscapes.
*   **And much more, to be announced in the coming months!**

![Image 3](https://images.nationalgeographic.org/dtpgi0zck/image/upload/t_news_ui_scale_by_height494/OceanShow_Flythrough_1?_a=DAJHqpE+ZAA0)

Visualizations by REDVERTEX, based on designs by Hickok Cole, Inc.

“For 136 years the National Geographic Society and its iconic yellow border have served as a global beacon for exploration, curiosity, innovation and wonder,” said Jean Case, chairman of the board of trustees of the National Geographic Society. “This new Museum of Exploration will build on that legacy, bringing all who visit the museum exciting opportunities to virtually travel to the front lines of the unknown with our Explorers, and help to inspire the next generation of changemakers.”

Education meets exploration at the Museum of Exploration, where learning experiences ignite curiosity and wonder in the Explorers of tomorrow. When school groups visit, they’ll cultivate their Explorer Mindset, the same attitudes and skills that drive Explorers to inquire, build knowledge, and think critically and creatively to solve the world’s most pressing problems.

![Image 4](https://images.nationalgeographic.org/dtpgi0zck/image/upload/t_news_ui_scale_by_height494/LearningLaunchpad_1?_a=DAJHqpE+ZAA0)

Visualizations by REDVERTEX, based on designs by Hickok Cole, Inc.

Inclusivity and accessibility have been instrumental in the museum’s design and visitor experience. Braille instructional text, tactile and sensory maps, intuitive app support with visual descriptions, American Sign Language (ASL) interpretations of media, refrigerators available for guest medication storage, all-gender restrooms, and wellness rooms that can be used for nursing and low-sensory time are some of the offerings available. All exhibition spaces will feature English and Spanish text, and the experience-based spaces will have Spanish subtitles. Resources will also be available in multiple additional languages.

“This experience is set to become a staple of the Washington, D.C. community — particularly within the Golden Triangle neighborhood — and it’s important we build upon our legacy as a historic institution in this city,” said Emily Dunham, chief campus and experiences officer at the National Geographic Society. “We are committed to making a positive impact at every level, inspiring the Explorer in all visitors and uniting the public on a common mission to become global stewards of our extraordinary planet.”

The Museum of Exploration will open its doors in 2026 to inspire current and future generations in the Washington, D.C. region and worldwide to learn about, care for and protect the planet. Visitors will leave knowing what it means to be an Explorer and that exploration is for everyone. They will be inspired to become explorers by engaging in, observing and documenting the world around us. Learn more at [natgeomuseum.org](https://www.nationalgeographic.org/society/museum-of-exploration/) and follow along for updates on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/NatGeoMuseum/) and [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/natgeomuseum/). For additional assets and information, please visit our [press kit](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Q-4V5DLaFqYsXQHmMyV_JRmIEw56-b5j?usp=drive_link).

Calling All Explorers
---------------------

Calling All Explorers
---------------------

[![Image 1](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/OceanShow_Flythrough_1-1024x576.jpg)](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/OceanShow_Flythrough_1-scaled.jpg)

Phase two of National Geographic’s headquarters renovation brings the Museum of Exploration to DC. National Geographic enlisted Hickok Cole and our engineering partners to reimagine the central plaza, expand the interior experience, and design a new pavilion that transforms the existing quiet entry into a dynamic destination in Washington,  DC.  The pavilion is a showcase for storytelling, exploration, and place where visitors, members, and explorers can all meet and interact.

Click on any image to open gallery.

[![Image 2](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Courtyard_Daytime_1-1024x724.jpg)](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Courtyard_Daytime_1-scaled.jpg)

Guided by National Geographic’s mission, to illuminate and protect the wonder of our world, we combined inspiration from nature with cutting-edge digital fabrication technologies to envision and then construct the unprecedented Museum of Exploration – a cultural landmark that sets new benchmarks in both scale and innovation.

A reimagined pedestrian pathway along the campus perimeter and rich, multi-sensory plaza environment activate the new campus gateway along the busy M Street corridor.

National Geographic’s iconic yellow border, referencing the design of its magazine, welcomes explorers to the campus and marks the beginning of the immersive experience.

[![Image 3](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Pavilion_Exterior_1-1024x576.jpg)](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Pavilion_Exterior_1-scaled.jpg)

Designed to present and preserve stories from National Geographic’s history, the space will feature immersive exhibits, a renovated theater, video wall, cutting-edge nighttime courtyard digital show, new store, a renovated café,  state-of-the-art education center, public archives and one of the key attractions—the Rolex Explorers Landing, an exhibition focused on storytelling of historic expeditions by engaging equipment and artifacts.

[![Image 4](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/HCA_NatGeoPavilion03_CGI07_06_Opt01-2048x1152.jpg)](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/HCA_NatGeoPavilion03_CGI07_06_Opt01-scaled.jpg)

[![Image 5](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/HCA_NatGeoPavilion03_CGI13_06-1024x576.jpg)](https://hickokcole.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/HCA_NatGeoPavilion03_CGI13_06-scaled.jpg)

Inclusivity and accessibility are woven and engrained into the museum’s design and visitor experience, ensuring the entirety of National Geographic’s audience are welcome to explore. Features such as braille instructional text, tactile and sensory maps, refrigerators available for medication storage, all-gender restrooms, and wellness rooms are available for guests to use.

“The Museum of Exploration marks a historic chapter in the Society’s mission to advance exploration, science, education and storytelling,” CEO Jill Tiefenthaler told the [Washington Business Journal](https://www.bizjournals.com/washington/news/2024/10/21/national-geographic-society-museum-of-exploration.html). Jean Case, Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the National Geographic Society, said in their press release, “This new Museum of Exploration will build upon that \[mission\], bringing all who visit the museum existing opportunities to virtually travel to the front lines of the unknown with our Explorers, and help to inspire the next generation of changemakers.”

The National Geographic Society Headquarters is a historic complex of buildings in Washington, D.C., United States. The complex was constructed in phases beginning in 1904 to house the offices and museum of the National Geographic Society, a scientific and educational nonprofit institution that has been headquartered in Washington since its 1888 founding. The historical portion of the site consists of three buildings: the 1904 original structure Hubbard Hall, the adjoining Administration Building, of which the north wing was constructed during 1912–1913, and the south wing and central pavilion in 1932; and the 1963–1964 Stone Building. A fourth building constructed in 1984 is too modern to be considered a contributing structure to the historical segment of the complex.
The National Geographic Society developed over time from a handful of Washington-area scientists into a substantial, internationally respected institution. The group's headquarters grew along with the society, with the progressively larger buildings eventually occupying an entire half of a city block. Their architectural styles evolved over time as well. All were designed by notable architects, and the 1963–64 Stone Building by Edward Durell Stone in particular is considered a quality example of the New Formalism style.
The complex was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2023.[2] Hubbard Hall and the Administration Building had previously been listed on the register as contributing structures to the Sixteenth Street Historic District.[3] The site is also listed on the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites.[4] As of 2025[update], the society still used the complex for its headquarters and was constructing a 2026 expansion on the site.

Location[edit]
The site comprises four buildings occupying the northern half of a long city block in central Washington, D.C., north of the White House.[2]: 5 [5] The eastern and western boundaries of the complex are 16th Street NW and 17th Street NW, respectively, while the northern boundary is formed by M Street and the southern by an alley bisecting the block. The original headquarters structure, Hubbard Hall, is located on the northeastern corner of the block with its main entrance facing 16th Street. The Administration Building, which also faces 16th Street, was constructed just south of Hubbard Hall and extends south to the alley. The Stone Building was built along 17th Street and changed the site's primary orientation by having its main entrance open on that roadway. The complex's fourth building, constructed after the site's period of historical significance, was built on the site between the older three structures. All four buildings are connected, either above or underground.[2]: 5

History[edit]
Establishment and first headquarters[edit]
The National Geographic Society (NGS) held its first meeting in January 1888 at the Cosmos Club, a private D.C. gentlemen's club aimed at "the advancement of its members in science, literature, and art".[6][7] The society itself stated in its bylaws the goal of achieving the "increase and diffusion of geographic knowledge".[8] The group began with 33 members,[6] many of whom were not scientists, including co-founder and first society president Gardiner Greene Hubbard.[9] Hubbard, a lawyer and recent transplant from Boston at the time of his election,[2]: 19  led the group until his death in 1897.[10]

A gathering on the front steps of Hubbard Hall. The group includes Roald Amundsen (marked #3 on the photo), Robert Peary (#4), Alexander Graham Bell (#7), and NGS director Gilbert H. Grosvenor (#10)
Hubbard was succeeded as president by Alexander Graham Bell.[2]: 19  The inventor had married Hubbard's daughter Mabel while the two were in Boston,[2]: 25  and Bell had been involved with the society since its early days.[2]: 27  Under Bell's leadership the NGS sought to become more populist.[9] The group had begun issuing a monthly magazine in 1896,[10] but its contents were highly technical – an early article was titled "The Classification of Geographic Forms by Genesis" – and readership suffered.[11][12] Bell hired the organization's first full-time employee, Gilbert H. Grosvenor, to take over as editor-in-chief of the magazine.[2]: 19  At Bell's direction, Grosvenor targeted a more general audience – partly by greatly increasing the amount of photography – while attempting not to, in Grosvenor's words, "lower the dignity of the Society".[9][10]
Bell and Grosvenor's changes were largely successful, and by 1900 the society's membership of roughly 2,700 was considered one of the highest of any of the world's scientific organizations. In that year Hubbard's heirs announced that they had purchased a site at the corner of 16th and M Streets for the purpose of establishing a headquarters for the society and as a memorial to its founder.[13] Originally expected to cost $40,000 (equivalent to $1.2 million in 2024), the building was planned to have office space for the society and its magazine as well as a lecture hall for the group's smaller, more technical presentations (their more popular lectures were being held at that time at a local church).[14]
Following a bidding process, the architectural firm of Hornblower & Marshall was chosen to design the new building, termed Hubbard Memorial Hall.[2]: 20  Mabel Bell was heavily involved with the planning process and had considerable influence over its final design.[15]: 180  The structure's cornerstone was laid in April 1902 and contains a box of documents concerning Hubbard's career and accomplishments.[15]: 180  The two-story building, which eventually cost over $75,000 to construct,[16] was sufficiently completed by October 1903 for its first floor offices to be occupied by the society's magazine,[17][18] though a formal opening ceremony was not held until March the following year. Prior to that reception, Bell hosted a dinner in honor of W.J. McGee, who was succeeding him as president.[16] Bell remained on the group's board of trustees and contributed regularly to its magazine until dying in 1922.[10]

Two-part expansion[edit]
Hubbard Hall and the 1913 annex, prior to the completion of the Administration Building
Membership in the NGS surpassed 100,000 in 1911, with the group adding 30,000 new members in that year alone,[19] and by 1913 the society was using two branch offices in D.C. to house the clerks necessary to manage its rapid growth.[20] In December 1912, the group's board of managers approved an expansion of its headquarters.[21] They hired Arthur B. Heaton to design a new building, which would technically be an annex as it was to be connected to Hubbard Hall via a hyphen.[12] Completed in October 1913 at a cost of $150,000,[21] the new structure stretched 80 feet (24 m) on 16th Street and 90 feet (27 m) to the rear. The building contained clerical and office space as well as a cafeteria, and included a large third-floor office for Grosvenor, by then the institution's director.[20]
As early as 1914, it was planned that the NGS would expand even further south on 16th Street. In that year they purchased an additional 137 feet (42 m) of frontage on the road with the eventual goal of constructing a 3,000-seat auditorium.[22][23] By 1915 Heaton had drawn plans for the building, which was to turn the 1913 annex into the northern wing of a two-wing structure, with the southern wing to be designed in a complementary but slightly varied style. An illustrated depiction from the time shows the building topped by a massive tower that would "serve as a central landmark on 16th street".[23] It was 1932, however, before any expansion on the site was completed, and both the tower and auditorium were gone from the final design.[24]

An artist's depiction of the planned Administration Building expansion
With its membership up to 1.25 million, the NGS announced its 16th Street expansion in April 1931.[25] Heaton was retained again along with the same builders who constructed the 1913 annex, and it was decided for the new construction to mirror that of 1913. The new construction would become the southern wing and central pavilion of the Administration Building, with the 1913 building becoming its northern wing.[2]: 9  Upon its completion it was announced that the society's scientific collections would be kept in the new structure, along with fireproof vaults housing the group's 300,000 photographs of the world's geography, reportedly the largest collection in the world at the time.[24] The magazine's editorial offices were to be moved to the building as well.[24] The organization later established an exhibition space in the building called Explorers Hall. The hall, which was free and open to the public during the week, housed a sampling of the group's holdings as well as occasional special exhibits.[26]

Stone Building and beyond[edit]
The society's membership continued to grow through the middle of the 20th century, and by the time of Grosvenor's 1954 retirement was up to 2.15 million.[27] In 1959 the group announced its intention to expand its headquarters again, this time by demolishing Hubbard Hall and building a new, seven-story building in its place. A legal hitch concerning a 1905 transfer of ownership required the society to get court approval to raze Hubbard Hall, which they were successful in attaining.[28] In March 1960, however, the NGS spent $1 million to purchase a four-story structure located at M and 17th Streets, behind its existing headquarters,[29] and in June they announced that the new headquarters building would be located there and Hubbard Hall would remain standing.[30]
The NGS hired the architect Edward Durell Stone to design their new building.[30] Stone worked in the New Formalism style, but intended for his design to meld with both the other NGS structures on the site and with Washington as a whole.[2]: 12  In his 1962 memoir The Evolution of an Architect, he wrote, "Since the Society is a national institution, it was felt that the building should reflect the dignity of official Washington."[31] Originally planned as eleven stories and anticipated to cost $5 million,[30] the completed building stood ten stories tall and cost nearly double the initial estimate.[32] Construction began in April 1961 and the finished structure was dedicated in January 1964.[33] President Lyndon B. Johnson spoke at the dedication ceremony and said of the new building, "This imposing home stands not as a monument to the past but as a testament of confidence in—and enthusiasm for—the future."[32] Following the dedication, The New York Times said that "many regard the [Stone Building] as the most distinguished example of modern architecture in Washington".[34] The building was Stone's first contribution to the architecture of Washington;[35]: 82  the 1971 Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on F Street was one of the architect's final major projects.[35]: 115

The interior of Explorers Hall in 1971
Explorers Hall was moved to the Stone Building and featured a rotating sphere measuring 11 feet (3.4 m) across and weighing 1,000 pounds (450 kg). An operator manning a control panel used various special effects to project educational imagery on the globe.[33] Also featured in the building was one of the first three Picturephone booths in the United States. Developed by Bell Laboratories, the machine allowed for video phone calls to either of the other booths located at the time in New York and Chicago. The booth in the Stone Building was open to the public and calls could be made at the rate of $16 for the first three minutes to New York and $21 for the same duration to Chicago. President Johnson's wife Lady Bird attended a 1964 inauguration ceremony for the new technology and made a call to the Bell Labs scientist Elizabeth A. Wood in New York.[36]
In 1978, both Hubbard Hall and the Administration Building were listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) as contributing structures to the Sixteenth Street Historic District.[3] Those buildings along with the Stone Building were collectively added to the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites in 2022 and to the NRHP in 2023.[4]
The headquarters has continued to expand since the completion of the Stone Building. Another new structure was constructed in 1984 between the Stone and Administration buildings.[2]: 14  The nonprofit institution, flush with capital and needing to spend it, paid the building's full $50 million cost with cash.[9] Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM), the seven-story building features horizontal massing with ziggurat-style setbacks. As it was less than 50 years old when the complex was listed on the NRHP, the SOM building is considered too modern to be a contributing structure to the site's historical status.[2]: 5  Hubbard Hall was renovated in 1984 as well, during which the five N.C. Wyeth murals located inside were professionally restored.[37]
By 2022, the site that had begun as a 7,659-square-foot (711.5 m2) building had grown by over 100 times to a complex the size of nearly 900,000 square feet (84,000 m2).[2]: 5 [5] In 2024 it was announced that the society was yet again expanding its campus – now nicknamed "Base Camp" – with the addition of a 100,000-square-foot (9,300 m2) museum.[38] According to the director of the group's building operations, the new construction "extends into the campus's four existing buildings" including Hubbard Hall.[39] Construction on the museum began in mid-2022 and as of October 2024[update] was scheduled to be completed in mid-2026.[38][39]

Architecture[edit]
Hubbard Hall[edit]
Hubbard Hall
The first purpose-built headquarters for the National Geographic Society was Hubbard Hall,[2]: 6  a two-story, three-bay structure.[2]: 18  It was designed by Hornblower & Marshall, a D.C.–based architectural firm responsible for a number of other listings on the National Register of Historic Places.[2]: 28  The firm chose an Italian Renaissance style for the building, which helped it fit into what was a primarily residential neighborhood while still giving the appearance of an institutional building.[2]: 5
The exterior is constructed with brick and both brick and mortar are buff-colored which makes the façade appear smooth. Limestone is used for detailing, and the hipped roof is red terracotta. The primary façade includes a first-floor central entrance flanked by two single windows. Above the entrance is a stone tablet that reads "NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY" in all capital letters. A row of decorative stone known as a stringcourse separates the first and second stories, above which are three large arched windows and a central Juliet balcony. Above the windows a horizontal strip, or frieze, is inscribed with "GARDINER GREENE HUBBARD MEMORIAL" in all capitals.[2]: 6
The building's north elevation facing M Street consists of three single windows on the first story and one large arched window on the second. The south elevation faces the 1912 Administration Building and features a recessed hyphen connecting the two. The west elevation has a two-story wing projecting from the building's central massing, and since 1984 has closely faced the fourth, most recent building in the complex.[2]: 7
The interior of the building includes a first-floor vestibule and foyer equipped with marble floors and walls and a marble split staircase ascending from the foyer.[2]: 8  The staircase's landings are painted with murals by the artist N.C. Wyeth that symbolize "the instinct for exploration and discovery".[40] The paintings were a late addition to the building, having been commissioned in 1926 and installed the following year.[15]: 187  The rest of the first floor originally held offices for the organization's board members, while a basement contained darkrooms and filing rooms for developing and storing the group's photography.[2]: 7  An auditorium and library shared a large second story room that later served as a board room and features a large carved stone fireplace.[2]: 7–8 [16]

Administration Building[edit]
The next building constructed in the complex was the Administration Building, which was designed by Arthur B. Heaton and built in two phases over a decade apart. The completed building is a four-story, Neoclassical structure consisting of a central pavilion flanked by five-bay wings. It is primarily constructed of buff-colored brick, which along with a similar red terracotta roof provides continuity with Hubbard Hall despite the change in architectural style.[2]: 9–10

Administration Building pavilion
The building's primary elevation faces east on 16th Street. Its entrance consists of three door openings cut into the pavilion's stone base and topped by a triangular enclosed pediment supported by Ionic columns that span the second and third stories. A frieze is carved with the words "NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY" in all capitals. The structure's wings are designed in the form of a classical column: a base consisting of the basement and first story, a shaft made of the second and third stories, and a fourth story capital. The base is separated from the upper levels by stringcourses. The shaft features double-height windows and giant order pilasters. A row of limestone molding known as a cornice projects below the capital, which consists of windows separated by limestone panels decorated with carved limestone rosettes.[2]: 10
The Administration Building contained offices for the society, and aside from the central lobby, the original floor plan and decorative elements have been much altered since its construction.[2]: 11  The lobby features at least six types of marble;[41] marble floors and walls are joined by red marble columns that extend upward to a plaster entablature and ceiling. A marble and brass world globe, the former logo of the society's magazine is embossed in the center of the floor and surrounded by a marble-laid star.[2]: 11 [41]

Stone Building[edit]
Stone Building
The Stone Building, also known as the Headquarters Building, was built between 1963–64. It was designed by Edward Durell Stone in the New Formalism style in an effort to create a modern building that still echoed the society's architectural history. The ten-story building is built of reinforced concrete covered with white marble cladding, and, like the society's previous Administration Building, is designed in the form of a classical column: a one-story base supports a nine-story shaft, topped by a flat-roofed capital. The building's primary elevation faces 17th Street, which re-oriented the complex's primary entrance from east to west.[2]: 12
The structure's ground floor exterior features an array of marble piers that support the building's canopy and form an arcade. The piers' resemblance to marble columns adds to the classicist appearance of the modernist building. The primary entrance on 17th Street is composed of centered pairs of bronze doors, above which is engraved "National Geographic Society". The building's shaft is made up of rows of narrow, bronze-framed windows flanked by marble "fins" projecting outward and separated horizontally by black granite spandrels. The design emphasizes the building's vertical composition. A flat, projecting roof caps the structure, which was an element Stone used often in his work.[2]: 12  All four of the building's elevations share the same design motif, and all four have ground floor entrances.[2]: 13
The building's interior was constructed with an array of office space, laboratories, exhibit halls, and a cafeteria. While most of the interior has since undergone considerable changes, the main lobby retains much of its original appearance and fixtures. It contains stone floors and marble walls, and features a brass globe in its floor much like the lobby of the Administration Building.[2]: 13

Every explorer needs a base camp, and the National Geographic Society’s headquarters have served as one for over a century. Starting in 2026, those headquarters will be home to a newly reimagined [National Geographic Museum of Exploration](https://news.nationalgeographic.org/national-geographic-society-introduces-the-museum-of-exploration/) when it opens in Washington, D.C.

Renovations are currently underway for the redesigned building to provide visitors with expanded museum space, immersive experiences, and a new education center. These changes are only the latest chapter in headquarters’ transformation over 120 years. As it expanded from a single structure to an entire campus, these buildings tell the story of both the Society and the city.

Here are five things that might surprise you about National Geographic’s historic headquarters—from a luxe fallout shelter and morgue to the colonies of bees that call it home.

1\. It was designed by the world’s leading architects
-----------------------------------------------------

The Society didn’t initially have a building of its own. Instead, members met at places like [Washington, D.C.’s Cosmos Club](https://www.cosmosclub.org/the-club/about-the-club/), where the organization was [founded in 1888](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/national-geographic-society-founded/).

The Society opened its own building in Washington in 1904. Named for the Society’s first president [Gardiner Greene Hubbard](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1622820), Hubbard Memorial Hall was only the first in what would become a complex in the heart of the city. The Society’s membership [ballooned from 2,700 to 150,000](https://books.google.com/books?id=_2dK3n--wAkC&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&pg=PA183#v=onepage&q&f=false) in just eight years, prompting them to erect a new building in 1912. More additions came in the 1960s and 1980s.

![Image 1: Black and white aerial photo of buildings surrounding a construction site.](https://i.natgeofe.com/n/e719a43e-18aa-47bc-8255-295fd48cbd57/NationalGeographic_785050.jpg)

The National Geographic Society began constructing a new wing of their 16th Street building in 1948. The 16th street building is part of the Society's ongoing headquarters renovation efforts.

Photograph by Luis Marden, Nat Geo Image Collection

Each expansion was overseen by renowned architects, most of whom designed other landmark buildings in Washington. Hornblower & Marshall, who designed Hubbard Memorial Hall, also designed the National Museum of Natural History. The architect behind the 1912 structure—Arthur B. Heaton—[built over a thousand buildings](https://books.google.com/books?id=zaojAQAAQBAJ&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&lpg=PP1&pg=PA266#v=onepage&q&f=false) in and around the city, including the Washington National Cathedral. Finally, the Society’s 1960s expansion was designed by Edward Durrel Stone, who would go on to design the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

[![Image 2](https://i.natgeofe.com/n/40eac27f-ce75-45c5-812c-5cc4e7fc20fa/NGM-International-15358_600x4001_3x2.jpg)](https://ngmintlsubs.nationalgeographic.com/SingleItem?item=Ngf&prom=I4MPYUGB&cmpid=int_org=ngp::int_mc=website::int_src=ngp::int_cmp=acq_holiday25_intl::int_add=inarticlepromo)

Get 2 Bonus Issues!
-------------------

This special offer is only available for the holidays. Subscribe to Nat Geo Digital + Print today!

Together, these architects helped define the look of Washington in the 20th century and stitched headquarters into the architectural fabric of the city.

2\. The FBI used it to spy on the Soviets during the Cold War
-------------------------------------------------------------

Headquarters’ proximity to the Soviet embassy—which was just down 16th Street—made it an unlikely front line during the Cold War. From the middle of the 1960s to the early 1970s, [FBI agents maintained a clandestine surveillance office inside the Society’s headquarters](https://books.google.com/books/about/Explorers_House.html?id=XdR-AAAAMAAJ) to spy on the nearby embassy. The FBI attempted to cover its tracks by calling its operations the “Mid-Atlantic Research Committee.”

([_What was the Cold War—and are we headed to another one?_](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/cold-war))

3\. The building once even had its own fallout shelter and morgue
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Another relic of the Cold War was a fallout shelter with a morgue that was constructed in the 17th Street building in the 1960s. The city was littered with such shelters, so it’s likely that this one catered primarily to Society staff, according to Society senior archivist [Cathy Hunter](https://www.linkedin.com/in/cathy-hunter-16905b10).

Unlike most of the spartan shelters in Washington at the time, the Society’s fallout shelter [had relatively plush amenities](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1982/06/02/no-good-place-to-hide/820738cf-8f53-4d2b-8b5f-5914247c6c2f/), including cots, showers, medical supplies, and toothpaste. “This is a five-star fallout shelter which, compared to others, could make nuclear war about as unpleasant as a stay at the Ritz,” opined a 1982 feature in _The Washington Post_.

4. It’s been a literal home to Explorers
----------------------------------------

Headquarters has served as a home base for the Society’s Explorers since the earliest days of the organization, when it supported the work of adventurers such as [Hiram Bingham](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/machu-picchu-hiram-bingham?loggedin=true&rnd=1729710647273), who explored Machu Picchu in the early 20th century. Society’s buildings have been the setting for lectures and receptions as Explorers bring back tales of their adventures.

![Image 3: National Geographic Explorer and his team arriving to camp in Ndoki, Congo.](https://i.natgeofe.com/n/4a4eb41a-bd50-4806-8992-867743bc7b7a/NationalGeographic_689018.jpg)

National Geographic Explorer Michael Fay and his team arrive at the Ndoki II logging camp in Congo. Explorers, including Fay, used National Geographic headquarters as a home during their research.

Photograph by Michael K. Nichols, Nat Geo Image Collection

Some Explorers have taken the concept of home base more literally. In the 2000s, conservationist [J. Michael Fay](https://explorers.nationalgeographic.org/directory/j-michael-fay) sometimes slept over in a Society building while in Washington. Known for his [Megatransect](https://www.instagram.com/natgeo/p/B_fOetpDURZ/) across the Congo Basin and his [Megaflyover](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/mike-fay-mega-flyover/) project to raise awareness about elephant poaching, Fay’s work aims to protect land and wildlife by highlighting the impact humans have had on the environment.

You May Also Like
-----------------

5. Headquarters is home to bees that visit the White House
----------------------------------------------------------

One balcony on the 16th Street building has been [home to bee colonies](https://www.tiktok.com/@natgeo/video/7364063302214749482) since 2011. The number of colonies varies every year, though each has around 50,000 bees.

Honeybees support biodiversity in urban spaces like Washington. They [pollinate flowers and trees throughout the city](https://www.americanforests.org/article/bees-and-cherry-blossoms-in-d-c-a-mutually-beneficial-relationship/), ensuring that iconic sites. One destination for them: the White House, which is less than a mile away and has 18 acres of flowering trees.

([_Inside the 18th-century contest to build the White House_](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/history-magazine/article/building-the-white-house).)

“We’re trying to make sure people recognize the importance of the world around us and how interconnected we all are,” says [Susan Kolodziejczyk](https://www.linkedin.com/in/susankolodziejczyk), the Society’s sustainability director. “Humans, animals, plants—without all those things, there’s a lot we would be missing.”

![Image 4: A close up photo of a group of bees.](https://i.natgeofe.com/n/fc1084ad-43da-49b2-a219-807227491c1d/NG_Bees_20171101_0188.jpg)

These European honeybees live on National Geographic's sixth floor balcony. The bee colonies add to National Geographic's mission to support biodiversity.

Photograph by Mark Thiessen, Nat Geo Image Collection

![Image 5: A man wearing a beekeeping suit while holding up a tray of bees on a balcony in Washington, DC.](https://i.natgeofe.com/n/d190295b-aa9d-4971-a2ca-236d45cfa007/Bees_20180515_0128.jpg)

National Geographic photographer and beekeeper Mark Thiessen holds a beehive from an apiary at Nat Geo's headquarters. Thiessen helps care for the colonies as the honey is harvested and bottled annually.

Photograph by Rebecca Hale, Nat Geo Image Collection

_National Geographic_ staff photographer [Mark Thiessen](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/podcasts/overheard/article/can-you-picture-that-this-photographer-can-and-does) acts as a volunteer beekeeper. Among his duties are feeding the bees sugar water and treating them for mites.

The amount of honey that the Society can harvest changes annually. “One year, it was 540 pounds of honey,” recalls Thiessen. What happens to it? Staff volunteers bottle it, and the Society uses it as gifts, prizes, and in menus—including ice cream and cocktails—for special events.

([_Move over, honeybees—America's 4,000 native bees need a day in the sun_](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/native-bees-pollinators-world-bee-day).)

Indeed, the opening of the reimagined National Geographic Museum of Exploration in 2026 promises to be one such special event, when headquarters will begin a new chapter in its remarkable history.
